quizName: DMV Practice Test #9 25 Questions • Passing Score 20

questions.question: What is the problem with riding alongside another rider?

options.text: It uses more of the road surface.
It limits your escape routes if you need to avoid a hazard.
It makes it easier to talk to the other rider.
It makes it easier for other cars to pass you.

questions.correctAnswerText: It limits your escape routes if you need to avoid a hazard.
questions.explanation: Do not ride alongside another motorcycle. This limits both riders' ways to escape if a hazard appears.

questions.question: When choosing a helmet, which of the following is NOT important?

options.text: It meets U.S. Department of Transportation standards.
It fits snugly.
It has no cracks or damage.
It looks attractive.

questions.correctAnswerText: It looks attractive.
questions.explanation: Choose a helmet that meets U.S. Department of Transportation and state standards. It must fit snugly and have no cracks, loose padding, or damaged straps. How it looks is not important for safety.

questions.question: What does making eye contact with another driver mean?

options.text: The driver sees you.
The driver may not yield to you even if they see you.
The driver will definitely yield to you.
The driver might become angry.

questions.correctAnswerText: The driver may not yield to you even if they see you.
questions.explanation: Never count on eye contact to mean a driver will yield to you. Drivers often look directly at motorcyclists but still do not see them.

questions.question: What does eye contact with another driver guarantee?

options.text: The driver will give you the right of way.
Nothing is worth the effort.
The driver may not yield to you even if they see you.
The driver knows you are there.

questions.correctAnswerText: The driver may not yield to you even if they see you.
questions.explanation: Never assume that eye contact with another driver means they will yield to you.

questions.question: Where should a passenger sit on a motorcycle with a sidecar?

options.text: On the motorcycle seat.
In the sidecar.
Either on the motorcycle or in the sidecar.
Neither on the motorcycle nor in the sidecar.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the sidecar.
questions.explanation: Your passenger should ride in the sidecar. They should keep their hands inside the sidecar at all times.

questions.question: If your motorcycle weaves while riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings, what should you do?

options.text: Relax, keep your speed steady, and ride straight across.
Grip the handlebars tighter and speed up to get past it.
Zigzag across the surface.
Ride on the shoulder instead.

questions.correctAnswerText: Relax, keep your speed steady, and ride straight across.
questions.explanation: Weaving over rain grooves or bridge gratings is usually not dangerous. Simply relax and ride straight across at a steady speed. Zigzagging is more dangerous than riding straight.

questions.question: Why should less experienced riders ride near the front of a group?

options.text: Experienced riders can watch them more easily.
They will get lost if they lead.
They might slow everyone down.
They will ride too fast in other positions.

questions.correctAnswerText: Experienced riders can watch them more easily.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride near the front, just behind the leader. This lets experienced riders watch them easily.

questions.question: Which of the following will NOT help prevent fatigue while riding?

options.text: Protecting yourself from wind, cold, and rain.
Using artificial stimulants like energy pills or drinks.
Limiting how far you ride in one day.
Taking frequent breaks.

questions.correctAnswerText: Using artificial stimulants like energy pills or drinks.
questions.explanation: Take frequent breaks and limit riding to six hours or less per day. Dress to protect yourself from wind, cold, and rain. Do not use artificial stimulants, as the danger increases when they wear off.

questions.question: Which of the following should your lane position NOT do?

options.text: Help you avoid road hazards.
Keep you out of other drivers' blind spots.
Make it harder for other drivers to see you.
Make it easier for others to see you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Make it harder for other drivers to see you.
questions.explanation: A good lane position helps you see and be seen. It keeps you out of blind spots, helps you avoid hazards, lets others know your plans, protects you from wind blasts, and gives you an escape route.

questions.question: When should you keep a larger space between you and the vehicle ahead?

options.text: When the road is wet or icy.
When it is sunny.
When the temperature is cold.
When you are following other motorcycles.

questions.correctAnswerText: When the road is wet or icy.
questions.explanation: A two-second following distance is normal. Use more space when conditions make it harder to stop, such as wet or icy roads.

questions.question: When carrying a passenger in a sidecar, you should:

options.text: Start slowing down sooner than usual.
Start slowing down later than usual.
Brake harder than usual to stop quickly.
Brake gently to avoid wearing out the brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Start slowing down sooner than usual.
questions.explanation: A passenger in a sidecar adds weight to your motorcycle. This extra weight means you need more space to stop completely.

questions.question: For routine braking:

options.text: Use only the front brake.
Use only the rear brake.
Switch between front and rear brakes to make them last longer.
Always use both the front and rear brakes together.

questions.correctAnswerText: Always use both the front and rear brakes together.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes every time you slow down or stop.

questions.question: When riding in fog, you should:

options.text: Use your high beam headlight.
Use your low beam headlight.
Ride with no lights.
Switch between low and high beams.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use your low beam headlight.
questions.explanation: Use your low beam headlight in fog. Do not use high beams when other vehicles are nearby.

questions.question: When an operator's left arm is extended straight out to the left, it means the operator:

options.text: Plans to turn left.
Is about to stop.
Plans to turn right.
Is about to slow down.

questions.correctAnswerText: Plans to turn left.
questions.explanation: Hand signals show your intentions instead of using turn signals. A left arm extended straight out means the operator plans to turn left or change lanes to the left.

questions.question: The front brake is:

options.text: Too dangerous for inexperienced riders.
Best when used alone.
Meant to help the rear brake only sometimes.
Meant to be used with the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Meant to be used with the rear brake.
questions.explanation: Use both the front and rear brakes every time you slow down or stop.

questions.question: All of the following reduce your chance of a crash, except:

options.text: Staying alert.
Spotting hazards and deciding which ones to handle first.
Riding without a headlight.
Keeping a safe distance around your motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Riding without a headlight.
questions.explanation: To reduce crash risk, stay alert and ready to react. Spot hazards and decide which ones matter most. Always use your headlight to be seen better and keep safe distance around your motorcycle.

questions.question: Most crashes happen during the day. To reduce your crash risk, you should:

options.text: Wear dark-colored clothing.
Wear bright-colored clothing.
Avoid riding during the day.
Choose safer routes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Wear bright-colored clothing.
questions.explanation: Make yourself as visible as possible by wearing bright-colored clothing when riding, even during the day.

questions.question: If your motorcycle starts to wobble, you should:

options.text: Speed up to stop the wobble.
Brake slowly.
Hold the handlebars firmly and slowly release the throttle.
Shift to a lower gear.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hold the handlebars firmly and slowly release the throttle.
questions.explanation: Speeding up will make the wobble worse and more dangerous. Instead, grip the handlebars firmly, slowly release the throttle to slow down, and lean forward and down. Pull off the road as soon as you can.

questions.question: When riding at night, you should:

options.text: Stay closer to the vehicle ahead.
Stay farther from the vehicle ahead.
Ride faster than usual.
Avoid using your high beam headlight.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay farther from the vehicle ahead.
questions.explanation: It is harder to judge distance in the dark. Slow down and increase your following distance when riding at night. Use your high beam whenever you are not meeting or following another vehicle.

questions.question: Which type of sign is yellow with black lettering or symbols?

options.text: Warning
Service
Regulatory
Speed limit

questions.correctAnswerText: Warning
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They alert drivers about upcoming road conditions.

questions.question: When changing lanes, what should riders do?

options.text: Only use mirrors to check for other vehicles.
Turn their head to look for traffic behind them.
Ignore other traffic.
Brake hard to let vehicles in blind spots pass.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn their head to look for traffic behind them.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles have blind spots like other vehicles. Always turn your head to check for traffic before changing lanes.

questions.question: Which of these should a face shield NOT be?

options.text: Free of scratches.
Able to provide clear views to the sides.
Airtight.
Fastened securely.

questions.correctAnswerText: Airtight.
questions.explanation: A good face shield should be scratch-free, let you see clearly to both sides, fasten securely, and allow air to flow through. An airtight shield can fog up and block your vision.

questions.question: When making a turn, how does stopping ability change?

options.text: There is less grip available for stopping.
There is more grip available for stopping.
Stopping works the same as on a straight road.
You should never try to stop while turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: There is less grip available for stopping.
questions.explanation: You can brake while turning, but be very careful. When leaning into a turn, some grip goes to the turn, leaving less grip for braking.

questions.question: What percentage of stopping power does the front brake provide?

options.text: About 25%
About 50%
About 75%

questions.correctAnswerText: About 75%
questions.explanation: The front brake is stronger than the rear brake. It gives about three-quarters of the motorcycle's total stopping power.

questions.question: Which item is NOT protective riding gear?

options.text: A leather jacket
Boots above the ankle
Hearing protection
Pants made of soft material

questions.correctAnswerText: Pants made of soft material
questions.explanation: Good protective gear includes a leather jacket or sturdy material; pants made of leather or other tough material; boots that cover the ankles; and hearing protection even with a helmet.
